title: Self-adaptive verifier-triggered orchestration for multi-agent workflows
research_question: Can a multi-agent workflow improve task success per token and reduce cascading errors by adding a self-adaptive control loop that selectively triggers verifier and replanning agents only when runtime signals indicate elevated decomposition or execution risk?
hypothesis: A MAPE-K-style controller that monitors intermediate agent traces, uncertainty proxies, and task-state inconsistencies can trigger verification and replanning more efficiently than always-on verification or static orchestration, yielding better success-cost tradeoffs on long-horizon tasks.
motivation: The knowledge base suggests a gap between mature self-adaptive control methods and current agentic workflow design. The self-adaptive systems literature explicitly highlights extending MAPE-K approaches to additional domains and to heterogeneous requirements, while the failure log shows that a generic Bayesian uncertainty-aware scheduler for multi-agent workflows was already rejected for insufficient novelty. This points to a more specific and publishable angle: not another generic uncertainty scheduler, but a self-adaptive orchestration mechanism that uses runtime signals to decide when to invoke verifier or replanning agents. This targets a practical pain point in agent systems—cascading errors from bad decompositions—while avoiding the previously rejected idea by focusing on adaptive intervention policies rather than broad Bayesian scheduling alone.
